title: Where Does Karma Persist?
summary: If memory is tied to neurons, where does karma persist?
summary_html: If memory is tied to neurons, where does karma persist?
content_html:
Where Does Karma Persist?

Memory (as neuroscience studies it) is neural and ends with the brain. Karma (as Buddhism frames it) is causal and persists not as stored episodes but as dispositions shaping new arising. These are different kinds of continuity; reconciling them requires distinguishing engrams from karmic seeds.

Memory = changes in neurons and synapses. When the brain dies, those engrams dissolve. From this perspective, there’s no scientific mechanism for “karma” to persist beyond death — it would need to be redefined in non-biological terms (e.g. social, cultural, genetic, epigenetic inheritance).

Buddhism distinguishes between memory (smṛti/sati) and karma (action and its results). Karma is not stored as “memory episodes” but as dispositions or seeds that condition future experience.

Key concepts:

Dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda): actions leave causal traces that condition new arising.

Ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness, Yogācāra): a subtle flow of consciousness where karmic “seeds” (bīja) are deposited — not memories, but potentials.

Rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi citta, Theravāda): the moment-to-moment continuity of mind carries karmic imprints into a new life.

So where does karma “persist”?

  • Not in the brain as neurons (those perish).
  • Not in a soul (Buddhism rejects ātman).

Rather, in the causal continuity of consciousness (vijñāna-santāna). Karma is understood as potential energy in the moral/causal field of existence. When conditions change (e.g. at death), these potentials condition the arising of a new stream of consciousness.

Reconciling science & dharma

Science: continuity of memory = neural. Karma in the Buddhist sense cannot be tested by neuroscience; only the observable effects of behavior (psychological, social, intergenerational).

Buddhism: continuity of karma = causal. It doesn’t depend on explicit memory; it is more like dispositions or biases that shape new arising.

Possible bridges:

Epigenetics: experiences can leave inheritable marks without encoding “memories.” Parental experiences can leave heritable marks (e.g., methylation) influencing offspring behavior/physiology — not memories, but biases.

Culture/social memory: actions shape the world and people around us, persisting beyond individual neurons. Our actions shape norms, institutions, and people around us; these outlive our neurons and condition future behavior. Again: not episodic recall, but persisting effects.

Phenomenological: karma is a way of naming the persistence of intentional patterns, even as personal memory fades.

Memory vs Karma — What Persists?

Dimension Neuroscience (Memory) Buddhism (Karma) Notes
Ontology Synaptic/circuit states (engrams) Causal tendencies (bīja/seeds) Different categories: physical traces vs dispositional potentials
Carrier Hippocampus↔cortex networks; striatum; cerebellum Stream of consciousness; ālayavijñāna (Yogācāra); rebirth‑linking (Theravāda) No eternal self (anattā)
Change over time Consolidation/reconsolidation; sleep replay Conditioned by intention and action (karma); dependent origination Both are dynamic, history‑dependent
At death Traces dissolve with brain Dispositions condition new arising Continuity ≠ recall
Evidence mode Empirical/biological (lesions, LTP) Scriptural/phenomenological/soteriological Different standards of proof
